prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and for its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells and in three-dimensional bismuth-based crystals

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I have moved my preferred configuration from magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) to topological insulators (B006), and I want to say plainly why. The Kane-Mele prediction of a time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator with protected helical edge states is a falsifiable statement that nature could have refused. It was confirmed in 2007 by the quantized edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells (Molenkamp) and then in three-dimensional Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 by angle-resolved photoemission (Hasan). The ARPES spectra of the surface Dirac cone were matched quantitatively by first-principles band-structure calculations, which is exactly the tie between calculation and measured spectra that I trust, and about twenty years of work on many material families and probes by independent groups has left the picture stable. Topological classification of band structure also changed how we search for materials with DFT. B006 is the only candidate on the shortlist that is both a verified discovery in condensed matter and fully mature. The 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type invariants; the Z2 insulator without an external field, realised in real materials, is a distinct and later discovery, and a citation naming the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe and bismuth-crystal observations makes that distinction explicit. I keep Hasan as the third name because the three-dimensional ARPES discovery is the part that made topological insulators into a materials class, and a prize without it would credit the two-dimensional edge physics only.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point and I do not think any three names close it. Eugene Mele wrote the 2005 papers with Kane and is hard to separate from him, so choosing Hasan over Mele is a judgement that the experimental discovery of the materials class outweighs the second theorist, and a reasonable colleague can decide the other way. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that told Molenkamp what to measure, Zhang is deceased, and Fu, Moore and Balents are outside the three-dimensional theory credit. There is also the objection that B006 continues a topic honoured in 2016. Finally, my own first choice, B017, still has a strong prediction-then-confirmation structure, so I am giving up something I believe in; I do so on maturity and clean attribution, not because the physics of moire graphene has weakened.

responses.point: Mehlig moved Mele into his trio in place of Hasan, arguing that Kane and Mele are inseparable on the 2005 papers and that 3D credit is diffuse because Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Roy all contributed.
responses.response: His argument is serious and I changed my own position partly because of how he and Olsson framed maturity: I now agree that B006 is ripe and B017 is not yet. On the third seat I come out differently. The three-dimensional theory is diffuse, but the experimental discovery is not; Hasan's ARPES on Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 is what turned the Z2 idea into a materials class that spectroscopy and DFT could address. If we drop Hasan we cite the idea and one 2D experiment and omit the discovery of the material family, which is the broadest impact. If the committee prefers Mele, I would not object and would still support B006, but then I would want the citation worded narrowly around the quantum spin Hall effect and HgTe, as he proposes, so that the 3D gap is acknowledged rather than hidden.

responses.point: Olsson makes her B006 support conditional on checking what Mele contributed in the 2005 papers, and in her response to me argued that B017 is a candidate for a few years from now because the correlated phases are not understood and the credited experimentalist is the group leader while Cao and Fatemi did the measurements.
responses.response: She asked me to show that the correlated-insulator and superconductivity results are settled by several independent groups, and I cannot show it to the standard I would want for a prize: reproduction is broad, but the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder still limit quantitative comparison between devices, and the three-name cut is awkward when the first-author experimentalists fall outside it. I concede that and have moved. On Mele, my reading is that the Kane-Mele 2005 quantum spin Hall paper and the Z2 paper are joint work, so he has a real claim to the theory; that is the reason I regard the third seat as an open choice between Hasan and Mele and would accept her judgement if her check comes out for Mele. I do not think the 2016 objection is fatal for the reason she gives, time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first on the magic-wavelength principle, independent reproduction at the 1e-18 level and a clean two-name credit, and suggests centring the citation on millimetre-scale relativistic redshift; she ranks B006 seventh.
responses.response: I take her answer to the novelty objection seriously: the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle for neutral atoms and not a better comb or ion trap, and I withdrew my earlier suggestion that the redefinition of the second should come first. The independent cross-comparisons are the confirmation I ask for. My remaining difficulty is the one she states herself, that so far the output is limits and consistency checks, and that I find a discovery of new quantum behaviour in a material class easier to defend to the public. I am moving B047 up to my second alternative and would support it as the better choice if the committee decides topological credit cannot be settled; I would only ask her why she ranks B006 as low as seventh given its confirmation record.

responses.point: Johansson prefers circuit QED, arguing that strong light-matter coupling in circuits is a different discovery from the 2025 macroscopic tunnelling prize, and accepts the Girvin and Huang gap and has disclosed his WACQT link.
responses.response: I accept that the 2004 strong-coupling discovery stands on its own and that the credited trio contains no 2025 laureate, so the overlap argument is a matter of how it reads and not of scientific priority. Taken together with the missing Girvin and Huang, and given his disclosed tie to the architecture, I still think it is best left for a later cycle; I keep it out of my alternatives for that reason. I did note in round 1 that he and I agree on the quality of B017; now I place B017 as a strong candidate for a few years from now.

uncertainties: Whether the third seat in B006 should be Hasan or Mele; I lean to Hasan for the 3D materials discovery but could be moved by Olsson's check of the 2005 papers.
Whether a citation naming the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation can absorb the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit without implying that the committee resolved priority.
How much weight the 2016 prize should carry; I judge the Z2 insulator without an external field to be distinct but I have not heard the experts in topological phases argue it.
How soon the pairing mechanism and reproducibility of magic-angle superconductivity will be settled, which determines whether B017 becomes the stronger choice in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan or the alternatives B017 and B047. My expertise in electronic-structure theory and ARPES spectroscopy overlaps with B006 and B017, which is expertise and not a conflict, but I disclose that this background shaped my weight on matching theory to spectra.
